tip: Dovremmo is the conditional of dovere and turns duty into advice: dovremmo partire = we should leave, softer than dobbiamo (we must).
Bisogna + infinitive means 'one must'; the conditional Bisognerebbe softens it to 'one should' or 'you ought to'.
The l' in l'acqua is a squeezed la or il before a vowel, so it hides the gender. Acqua is feminine, shown by the -a in fredda.
Italian usually drops subject pronouns: 'mangio la pasta' is more natural than 'io mangio'. Use 'io' only for emphasis or contrast.
The Italian present covers both English tenses: compro il pane = I buy and I am buying bread.
Regular -are verbs take -i for tu: cucinare becomes tu cucini = you cook.
Every noi form ends in -iamo, whatever the verb group: noi prepariamo = we prepare.
'Con + noun' forms adverbial phrases: 'con attenzione' (carefully), 'con calma' (calmly). Alternative to -mente adverbs.
In centro takes no article, where English says in THE center. Italian keeps it bare: in centro, not in il centro.
Some -ire verbs insert -isc- in the singular: preferire gives lei preferisce. Same pattern as finire and capire.
Italian keeps the article for things loved in general: amo la musica, literally 'I love the music', even though English drops the.
Giocare takes a before a sport: gioco a tennis. English 'play tennis' has no preposition, but Italian needs the a.
gli is the masculine plural the before a vowel or s plus consonant: gli occhiali = the glasses. Otherwise it is i.
To say yes or no, Italian adds di: dice di no = she says no, direi di si = I would say yes.
bere is irregular with a hidden v: bevo, bevi, lui beve = he drinks. The stem is bev-.
'A' before cities: 'abitano a Roma'. Use 'in' before countries: 'in Italia'. The preposition depends on city vs. country.
gg before i sounds like the English j: leggi = you read, said LEDJ-ee. Before a or o it hardens.
'In' before countries: 'vive in Italia'. Use 'a' before cities. No article needed with 'in' + country name.
'Ascoltare' = to listen to. The 'to' is built in: 'ascolta la musica'. No preposition needed.
da marks from or a starting point: lavoro da casa = I work from home.
'A casa' = at home / homeward. 'Tornare a casa' = to go back home. No article needed with 'casa' in this set phrase.
pagare takes a direct object with no for: pago il conto = I pay the bill, pago il caffe = I pay for the coffee.
Drop the article before a singular family member with a possessive: tua madre = your mother, not la tua madre.
rispondere needs a before its object: risponde al telefono = he answers the phone. al = a plus il.
portare covers bring, carry, and wear at once: porto un regalo = I bring a gift, porto gli occhiali = I wear glasses.
macchina literally means machine, but in everyday speech it means car: guidi la macchina = you drive the car.
Alzarsi literally means 'raise yourself': ti alzi = you get up. The pronoun ti matches the subject tu.
'Credere in' = to believe in. 'Credere a' = to believe someone. The preposition changes the meaning.
sperare joins a following verb with di: spera di vincere = he hopes to win.
Loanwords like email do not add -s in the plural; the number shows on the adjective: molte email = many emails.
